en: Composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànrán of the Tang Dynasty.
Commentary on the "Vision of the Jeweled Stūpa" Chapter.
Regarding the four instances in this chapter where it says "vision of the jeweled stūpa," the subsequent text refers to these as "four rounds," which correspond to the four *siddhāntas*.

Furthermore, initially, the names translated as "existence" and "non-existence" differ across the three periods of time; because one necessarily rejoices upon seeing [the Buddha], this is called the "World.

As for the statement, "The Sūtra says that the Buddha has three bodies," this borrows from the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra* (Puxian guan jing); since it concludes this very sūtra, it can serve as corroborating evidence.

Regarding the phrase "the same shall apply to the Buddha," whenever there is a place in the future where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is being preached, this stūpa will reappear and that Buddha will also sit [there].
The original treatise also states: "This sūtra is for the sake of the enlightenment of the three bodies (*trikāya-bodhi*)."
"This sutra has already explained the cause and effect between teacher and disciple; therefore, it is the ancient Buddhas who witness and assemble the emanated Buddhas.

That *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* adds four Bodhisattvas to explain the cause and effect of Bodhisattvas; those who can add [to the assembly] are merely the manifested Buddhas acting as principal and associates. Thus, it does not require the assembly of [all] Buddhas, but simply states that throughout the ten directions they act as mutual principals and associates. Furthermore, it does not say that these associates are emanations of the Buddha, but refers to them merely as "retinues."
In all the chapters of the text, it is stated that "all the bodhisattvas were assembled.
The commentators remark: "The Way neither exists nor perishes; past and present are of one principle.

Thus, the splitting of the earth and the leaping forth of the stupa serve to manifest that the Twin Śāla trees do not perish; furthermore, the prolonging of the shadow and the subtle manifestation of the sixteen-foot form show that he was not born. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa."

Now, if one says that the stupa of an ancient Buddha is where a present Buddha sits, this signifies that the true Way of past and present is unborn; it does not necessarily prefigure the non-extinction at the Twin Trees.
Viewed superficially, it might be said that the present manifest Buddha enters the stupa of the ancient extinguished Buddha to signify extinction and non-extinction.

Now, I say this is not so: the Buddhas of antiquity manifested their entry into stupas to demonstrate extinction, yet they did not truly extinguish; Śākyamuni entered the stupa to manifest birth, yet he was not truly born. Because he is neither born nor extinguished, his sitting side-by-side with them symbolizes this.

The assembly gathers the emanations to summon their original counterparts; this reveals that Vairocana is not something newly produced. How could it be that only the sixteen-foot form manifests extinction for others?
A question is asked:
"When the great assembly beholds the stupa, is it the root or the consciousness?"
To build a stupa for others to see?

To extensively employ various analogies to refute both self and other—this demonstrates a profound failure to understand the great purport of the sutra. Following the three turnings of the wheel, even ordinary beings attained a vision distinct from their usual mundane perceptions; yet, since the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*’s contemplation of phenomena was intended for those of dull faculties in the final age, why would such a method have been necessary as a skillful means for the Buddha’s own contemporaries?
The principle underlying the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) of this sutra should likewise be understood as such.
Generally, if one lacks a comprehensive vision when interpreting the sutras, it will cause later students to remain unacquainted with the path of the school’s tenets;
I now provide this primarily to authenticate the sutra while incidentally discussing what is therein expressed.
Someone asked:
"When the ancient Buddhas are summoned and their emanations assembled, why are their bodies many while the stupa is one?

To answer this now, it is because the meaning of the sūtra is fully realized that the precious stupa is not multiple; and because it accords with the vow of Prabhūtaratna, the emanations are not manifold.
If it were necessary to assemble many stupas in order to realize the sutras, would the stupas not then be numerous?

Since [the Buddha] can manifest throughout the ten directions, we know with certainty that the stupas are likewise not one; therefore, while the division of bodies is an emanation, the stupas are likewise appropriate as provisional manifestations.
Now, following what is symbolized: the fact that the single body of the present Buddha manifests as many bodies secretly signifies that its manifested functions are not one;

the fact that the many stupas of ancient Buddhas show only a single stupa clearly signifies that the ultimate principle is non-dual. Moreover, the fact that they arise from the earth and ascend into space, along with all their various adornments, is by no means in vain.

Regarding "making this matter manifest": the turning of the wheel of Dharma by all Buddhas of the three periods of time and other such events ultimately culminate in the teaching of the appearance of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in the world; therefore, the text of the present sutra adds four points of inquiry to clarify this.
Regarding the phrase "The *Ratnavyūha* for the sake of beings," this refers to generating wholesome roots through the comparative measurement of merit.
As for the passage beginning with "Subhūti’s Inquiry" and so forth, the ninth chapter, the "Chapter on the Offering of Relics," states:
"The Buddha, due to Subhūti’s question, [considered whether] the merit from offering a whole [relic] and that from offering a fragment are identical or distinct in producing the Dharma."
The Buddha extensively compared and measured this, saying:

"Even if one were to build stupas filled with the relics of a single Buddha to cover an entire four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*), it would not equal the merit of making offerings to the living body (*saṃbhogakāya*); for it is because the physical body (*rūpakāya*) possesses relics."

Furthermore, to erect stupas filling the great trichiliocosm and making offerings to the *rūpakāya* (physical body) is not as meritorious as making offerings to the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body), because it is by virtue of the *dharmakāya* that the *rūpakāya* exists.

One should know that seeing the physical form does not equal hearing the sutras; for since the *dharmakāya* exists through hearing the sutras, the merit of the partial and the complete aspects of the sutras—namely, the *rūpakāya* and the *dharmakāya* respectively—is unequal.

Regarding the phrase "Crown King" (*Mūrdhābhiṣeka*) and so forth: I have previously examined the *Mahāyāna-mūrdhābhiṣeka-sūtra* and the *Vaipulya-mūrdhābhiṣeka-sūtra*, each in one fascicle, but this [text] was not found therein.
The meaning of the objection is: Since the teaching and the bestowal of the śarīra are identical in their timing and benefit, how can they not be equal?
The meaning of the response is: Although the timing of the bestowal of the śarīra is the same, it also arises from the power of the physical body.

The phrase "the masters of the Northern Land" [refers to those who] refute errors and reject what is incorrect; in meaning, this corresponds to the destruction of evil, which is precisely the application of antidotes.
The expression "having finished expounding the sutra" means that the main body of the scripture has been completed.
The "Earth Master" (Dishī) departs from the non-duality of the manifest body; because he accords with principle, he belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The "Commentary on the Treatise" (Shìlùn) below refutes the Earth Master’s error.
"The Master’s words" refer to Nanyue.
Although he speaks of the "three bodies," his intent is to use the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* to refute the Master of the Earth (Dizang).
"No coming" means it is not appropriate to come from the east; "no emerging" means it should not emerge by leaping forth.
Regarding the term "lofty," it should not be placed inside the stūpa.
Regarding the "response body" (nirmāṇakāya), it should not be understood as being limited to this alone.

As for the phrase "if it were this very [body]," etc., it refers to the superior characteristics of the three bodies as described by Nanyue; if one were to simply state that Prabhūtaratna is the Dharma-body Buddha, that would certainly be incorrect.
Since it is not even the *saṃbhogakāya*, how could it possess the three bodies?
Therefore, one should know that the claim that Prabhūtaratna is the *dharmakāya* does not fully capture the intent of the sūtra.
Regarding the phrase "merely indicating," it is appropriate to say that Śākyamuni and others merely use phenomena to indicate the principle.
Therefore, we know that his coming is not merely to bear witness, but to manifest the permanence of the Dharma; thus, Prabhūtaratna symbolizes the Dharma and possesses the three bodies.
Although Prabhūtaratna has long since entered extinction, his appearance now to testify to the sutra signifies that which is neither born nor extinguished;
though he passed into nirvana in the past, he still manifests his entire body, signifying that extinction is not true extinction.
Since it is neither arising nor ceasing, its permanence and immutability can represent the *dharmakāya*.
Śākyamuni’s entry into the stūpa makes the two bodies correspond to one another; because wisdom corresponds to its object, this can represent the *saṃbhogakāya*.

The manifestation of emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) represents the spontaneous realization of principle and phenomena; because the object and wisdom are in mutual resonance, they are able to give rise to these manifestations.

Regarding the passage from "the three Buddhas" to "neither identical nor different": they are not identical because each of the three [bodies] manifests its own three [aspects]; they are not different because within each of those three, all are one.
Furthermore, it can express that because the three characteristics are distinct, they are not one; yet because the substance of the phenomena is identical, they are not different.
Moreover, that which is expressed also does not differ because its substance is identical, but is not one because the bodies [of the individuals] are distinct.
Furthermore, because their modes of transformation differ, they are not one; because they collectively accomplish this [same goal], they are not different.
In summary, because they are three yet one, they are not different; because they are one yet three, they are not one.

Regarding the phrase "as stated below" under the section "Seeing the Jeweled Stūpa," the four characteristics are explicitly revealed in the preceding four passages to resolve those four texts; this is roughly as explained previously, and all four belong to the Perfect [Teaching].
From the section "The Stūpa emerges as two" onwards, the text next addresses the provisional and ultimate teachings (kyō-hon-jaku).
First, both meanings are presented together; second, the two intentions are explained.
Within the explanation, there are four parts:

First is the formal explanation; second, from "If the stūpa rises from the ground" onwards, is the differentiation of similarities and differences; third, from "If the stūpa comes" onwards, is the judgment regarding the exoteric and esoteric; fourth, from "Now we take" onwards, is the resolution of objections.
The initial section also has two parts:
first, clarifying the emergence of the stupa to corroborate what precedes and initiate what follows;
second, clarifying its presence in the air to manifest two meanings.
Therefore, both passages serve to corroborate what precedes regarding the provisional teaching (jiàojiào), while initiating what follows regarding the fundamental and the manifested (běnjì).
Within the first section, which corroborates what precedes, there are two parts:
first, concerning the ultimate reality (zhēnshí); second, concerning great wisdom (dàhuì). These two constitute the testimony of Prabhūtaratna.
The initial section has three parts:

first, showing that the three weeks are none other than the perfect reality; second, distinguishing between the extensive and abbreviated versions; third, indicating the circulation [of the teaching].
The first part follows the text. Regarding the second part: first comes the abbreviated version, followed by the extensive one.

Regarding the initial passage: since it is a reiteration of the proof, it may be treated briefly; thus, it simply says "the reality" (*tattva*). Furthermore, both the intermediate and extensive expositions concern that which is negated; while that which is negated is necessarily manifold, the negating subject is unique. Therefore, throughout the three turnings of the wheel—whether they consist of four, one, ten, or many elements—they do not transcend the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Next, regarding the "Eight Negations" mentioned in the middle section of the middle [division], this is fully explained as cited from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.

Because the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* reveals the ultimate principle, it praises the Buddha with the Eight Negations; likewise, the stupa that attests to the Middle Way Sutra also praises the reality with the Eight Negations. Thus, the event of the stupa’s emergence further symbolizes the Eight Negations because their meanings are identical; hence it is said, "The stupa rose from the earth," and so forth.
"Furthermore, 'the proof' [in the following section] below demonstrates that the circulation [of this text] is also authentic.
Question:
Why is there no proof for the Preface?
Answer: Since these two sections are real, how could their sequence be false?
If that is so, why does [the teaching] not wait until the end of the "Peaceful Practices" chapter and the beginning of the "Emergence" chapter?

Answer: Because the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta* fully elucidates the methods and regulations for persons and the Dharma, as well as the causes and effects of teachers and disciples in the present and future, along with their respective locations; and because the devas and nāgas provide protection and transform people to gather for the hearing [of the teaching], it is sufficient to distinguish the propagation of the sutra. Therefore, Many Treasures appears to bear witness. Having witnessed it, he commands the search for a person capable of propagating and transmitting it; thus, he brings Sadāprarudita to bear witness, thereby benefiting the present Buddha and exhorting the circulation [of the sutra]. Furthermore, by citing the person from the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta*, he bears witness to the propagator and exhorts the circulation.
Nevertheless, as there has not yet been a method for initiating the practice of wide propagation, the "Peaceful Practices" (Anle-xing) are reiterated.
Thus, the "Peaceful Practices" chapter is not yet connected to the "Emergence from the Earth" (Yongchu) chapter.

Next, regarding the reference to Mahāmati: as for "the truth," although it generally encompasses all four [truths], specifically it refers to that which is manifested; therefore, he first praises Mahāmati, and subsequently praises the Dharma that is spoken and manifested.

Mahāmati, this is precisely the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), which has already been fully explained previously; now, it merely serves to distinguish the similarities and differences between this and the non-common prajñā.
Within this, first comes the question; next, from "The Commentary" (*śāstra*) onwards, is the answer; and third, from "Just as... onwards, is the analogy.
Because both that *prajñā* and this *mahāmatis* are capable of entering [the truth], the term "wondrous dharma" (*saddharma*) partially applies to both wisdom (*jñāna*).
Regarding the section beginning with "One should know," the concluding meaning of these two passages is the same.
Next, regarding "arising after clarifying the fundamental": in contrast to the traces, one may speak of the fundamental and the trace (*honji-suijaku*).
This section is divided into two parts; first, it clarifies the cause for the arising [of the traces].

Because the stūpa emerged, he requested it to open; because the stūpa opened, he beheld the Buddha; because he beheld the Buddha, he requested his empowerment; because he received that empowerment, he stood in the air; because he stood in the air, he summoned the assembly; because he summoned the assembly, his voice reached them; because his voice reached them, the assembly arrived; because the assembly arrived, doubt arose; and because doubt arose, [the Buddha] was able to preach.

Regarding the phrase "clarifying the profound" (*mingxuan*) and so forth: this briefly cites the title of the sutra, as the term "profound" encompasses the entire work; thus it says, "The Buddha wishes to use this wondrous Dharma," and so on.
The section beginning with "For a long time" clarifies that which gives rise to what is manifested, manifesting the benefits across the three periods of time in the original ground.

Because it has been extinguished for a long time and now emerges, it is called "supernatural power" (*abhijñā*); because its present benefit lies in the teaching, it is called "sound"; and because its vows do not cease until the end of the future, it extends to the limits of the future. Since this gives rise to that, it is termed "opening."
Question:

The sutra merely states, "The Great Wisdom is the reality. Since there are passages where it is said that one emerges because of hearing the teaching, why do you say it "proves what precedes" and "gives rise to what follows"?

Answer: While the words [of the preceding section] lack explicit reasoning, the underlying principle exists; for from within this [section], one subsequently gives praise to the reality [itself]. Thus, it is known that what is established here serves as the basis for what follows, just as the arising of clarity is itself the arising of what comes after.
Next, regarding "in the air," the first part is explained according to the teaching, while "the persons of the seven stages of expedient means" refers to the perfection of their vision of principle.
Next, from "cultivated and attained" onwards, it concerns the original and the manifested (honji-suijaku).
Furthermore, the former section first narrates the traces (the phenomenal manifestations), while the subsequent passage beginning with "If one arouses... clarifies the fundamental nature.

Since it is stated in the commentary on the contemplation of the mind that "one cultivates contemplation based on the sūtras," one should know that every sūtra is suitable for practice. Yet, alas, the commentaries and sub-commentaries do not address this at all. Therefore, the practitioners and scholars of this school maintain both conduct and understanding without neglect, and the two meanings of "explaining the principles" and "contemplating the text" remain intact. I hope that those who cherish the Way will honor this!
Shangzhi! Every time I behold this principle, I regret that I have not yet partaken of it myself. I have lingered over it, contemplating it deeply, and shall carry it upon my head for all eternity.

Within this section of three parts, the first clarifies that each of the three bodies has both a signifier and a signified; it first explains how taking contemplation as the cause leads to the fruit of the Dharma-body. Since one does not possess only the Dharma-body at the moment of attaining it, it is said that "object and wisdom must coincide."

"Like a stūpa" below represents the [manifesting] capacity; "object and wisdom" below represents the *saṃbhogakāya*; "like Śākyamuni" below represents the [manifesting] capacity; "by means of the great reward" below represents the *nirmāṇakāya*; and "like the emanated bodies" below represents the [manifesting] capacity.

Next, from "By means of Prabhūtaratna" onwards, the manifesting agents are collectively cited; one should know that with respect to the practice of upholding the sutra through contemplation, the three bodies are fully realized.
Third, from "Samantabhadra" onwards, scriptural evidence is adduced; the attainment of these three kinds of bodies all belongs to the Vaipulya Mahāyāna teachings.

Next, from "There is a person" onwards, the text of the Old Translation (Jiufen) is presented; here it should state that there are sixteen chapters, whereas previously, from Maitreya’s question onwards, there were only ten chapters—this is the intention of Longyi of Mount Lu.
Regarding the phrase "too early," one should explain the boundaries of the preceding and following contexts to demonstrate that this master’s division of the text is premature.
This is similar to the refutation of Guangzhai’s speculative views; here, the critique is made based on the names of the "original" (hon) and the "traced" (ji).

However, according to this master’s intention, regarding the provisional application based on the person, he takes Prabhūtaratna as the fundamental (hon) and Śākyamuni as the trace (jaku). As for the previous application based on the speaker, it was Śākyamuni himself who spoke the three cycles of revelation, the opening of the provisional, and the circulation of the teaching. Now, the reason why [the master] refutes the designation based on the name is that this master does not realize that this sutra reveals the remote [meaning] which is absent in all other sutras; rather, he expects that only within the entire lifetime of the Buddha's teaching and specifically within the preceding *jaku-mon* (trace gate) can the original name be accepted. Why, then, must one speak of "fundamental and trace" (*hon-jaku*) at this very point?
If one were to anticipate the implicit meaning here, it would be acceptable; however, to do so within this specific textual section would be premature.

Regarding the phrase "a stupa made of the seven treasures," these refer to the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga) and the seven noble riches (saptāryadhanāni). The seven noble riches are: hearing, faith, precepts, concentration, diligence, relinquishment, and shame. One clarifies the varying depths of these seven according to their respective stages of teaching. Since these are both the seven [treasures] of the Buddha’s stupa and the realization of the sutras, they employ the seven factors of enlightenment and the seven riches of non-action (avijñapti). Within non-action, one must still possess innate virtue (prakṛti-guṇa), let alone that which is acquired through cultivation.

Because they are both cultivated and attained together with the seven noble treasures of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga-āryadhana*), although the precious objects are distinct, the seven treasures and the stūpa are not separate in terms of subject and object; nevertheless, the stūpa is the basis (*āśraya*) and the adornments are that which depends upon it (*āśrita*).

Regarding the phrase "five hundred high" and so forth: since the symbolism of the stupa must be explained comprehensively, "vertical" refers to looking toward the fruit from within the causal stage—wherein the ten thousand practices, even a single practice, or all practices, correspond to the ten thousand virtues, even a single virtue, or all virtues within the fruition of cause and effect. This progression from beginning to end is called "vertical. Being fully endowed within each respective state is called "horizontal. All practices whatsoever—whether traversing conditions, confronting objects, or the contemplation of the truths, the bases of power, and the perfections—all serve as adornments leading from cause to fruit. Whether horizontal or vertical, they must possess a substantial essence (*tattva*) before they can be termed the "adornment of the ten thousand virtues."

Regarding the phrase "the ground" which "abides in the emptiness of the ultimate truth": since the essence of ignorance is itself the emptiness of the ultimate truth, ignorance has nothing to be destroyed and nothing in which to abide; therefore, the emptiness of the ultimate truth has no capacity to abide.
Because there is nothing that can abide, the ground is already broken despite being unbroken, and emptiness is already abiding despite being non-abiding.
Regarding the phrase "various kinds" and so forth: concentration and wisdom are not many; they are spoken of in contrast to darkness and distraction.
Furthermore, because concentration and wisdom universally encompass all things,
they are also said to be "many," as explained in detail in the section on the "Inclusion of Dharmas" in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe Zhiguan).
Regarding the phrase "the chamber of immeasurable compassion," it is called a "chamber-grotto" (*kansi*) because the grotto itself serves as the chamber.
The phrase "it is also" is a reiterative explanation of the chamber.
A chamber is also called a house (*śālā*), and a banner is of the same category as a flag, as explained in the *Mahā-śreṣṭhī* [Sūtra].

Regarding the phrase "hanging down jewels" and so forth: from cause to fruit, all the virtues of the fruit depend upon the myriad practices within the cause; because they serve as adornments, they are able to transform those below, just as ornaments hang down once they have been completed.
Regarding the phrase "the four directions" and so forth, this refers to the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Through the winds of the path of the four directions of the Four Noble Truths, the fragrance of the four virtues of the four directions is blown forth, filling and pervading everywhere; this is the principle of the natural four virtues, which are made to spread far and wide by means of the provisional cultivation of virtues.
Regarding the phrase "there are two kinds of equality": "equality of dharmas" refers to the principle contemplated by Mahāmati;
"attaining together" refers to all [beings] reaching the fruit by means of the causal principle.
If the principle being contemplated were different from that of sentient beings, it would not be called "Great Wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "in such and such a way" and so forth: "first, in accordance with the characteristics of phenomena" praises the Buddha’s teaching because it accords with reality; "second, in accordance with their faculties and natures" refers to the fifth period [of the Dharma], because at that time the capacity of the audience was not missed.
Regarding the section "First, answering the second question": In the first question it was said that [the earth] "leapt up," whereas here it says "from the east.
Why is this? Answer:

The "east" describes the original conditions, while the "leaping up" expresses the fulfillment of former vows. As for what they represent: the "direction" represents the beginning, while the "leaping up of the earth" represents its manifestation.
Regarding the phrase "addresses the bhikṣus" and so forth, this serves as proof that the fourfold assembly was complete and that the Dharma was not being preached in their absence.
As for the words "it must be Many Treasures," a question is raised:

Among the Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions, could there not be even one who has not attained the manifestation of the [Dharma-body]? If those who have not yet manifested it should all be required to make a vow, why is it that only Many Treasures is singled out?
If one does not make a vow, one's path to Buddhahood will differ; if one makes a vow, all are entitled to hear the sutra.

Furthermore, the transformations of all Buddhas are preceded by their foresight of the capacities of beings; how could it be that they have already attained Buddhahood yet fail to reveal and manifest [the truth] until only after they have made a vow?
Answer:
Whether they are alike or different, open or closed, having vows or lacking vows—all these follow conditions.
If it is appropriate for those with vows to come, they will all arrive; why worry that they will not assemble?
The subsequent formulation of vows is likewise for the purpose of discerning objects.
Regarding the statement, "The three transformations of the pure land arise from the *pratisamvid* (liberations)," a question is raised:
Since the Buddha possesses the power of the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*, why does he still employ the mundane dhyāna of the Hīnayāna?
Furthermore, it is shown that [this state] destroys the three delusions and is not something to be remedied. Answer:

This is the fruit achieved by embracing the causes through the holy practices of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). At the stage of fruition, the functional activity of the result does not deviate from principle; it is precisely as described in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* regarding the possession of all *samādhis*. It is not a case of perceiving the dharma-realm of meditation during former causal times—how could the "liberations" (*vimokṣa*) and so forth transform the three thousand worlds?

However, since the matters concerning the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation Buddha) should be appended to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* likewise follows the Small Vehicle therein; thus it says: "If one wishes to attain mastery, one cultivates the *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery); if one wishes to attain vast universality, one cultivates the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality bases). If these were used only according to the Small Vehicle, they would apply solely to the trichiliocosm."

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "first, one transformation" which indicates the shattering of the three delusions: since these are matters that accord with principle within the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is not at all precluded that each and every one of them shatters the three delusions;
how much more so now, as this samādhi directly discusses its functional efficacy, where the shattering of delusions is merely what is being illustrated.

The preceding refutation has already been expressed, and the following is further refuted; for instance, regarding one who gives their consent (*chanda*) within the Saṃgha, they do not necessarily perform all the ritual acts of the Saṃgha in exactly the same way, which is why it is said "like" [the Saṃgha].

Because the vow-power of Prabhūtaratna required the assembly of all Buddhas, and furthermore so that the members of the congregations would know the great number of the divided bodies, these Buddhas opened the stupa and assembled; yet, as they did not actually arrive but merely dispatched their attendants to convey greetings and inquiries—much like the formal procedure of granting consent (*chanda*)—the attendants simply extended their salutations and offered no words of formal consent.

Regarding the phrase "the great assembly of various Buddhas granting their consent": within the Great Void Pavilion of the two realms of desire and form, all Buddhas of the ten directions are gathered extensively.
Twenty-one: "In the south there is a Buddha named Suvarṇagarbha. When the bodhisattvas there saw the light, they questioned that Buddha, and the Buddha replied:"
In the world of the north there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni; desiring to preach the Dharma for the great assembly to shatter their great arrogance, he has sent an envoy to me requesting offerings.
"I shall now grant it to him.

It shall be the same for other regions as well; let each have one great bodhisattva, accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, come here to offer praise with these verses, and there shall be no other words of desire."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) also records that one thousand Buddhas spoke in unison.

Now that the provisional [teachings] have been opened, he next wishes to manifest the ultimate, so as to show that the paths of all Buddhas are identical; therefore, he causes all the Buddhas to grant their consent (*anumodana*).
Someone asked:
"If all beings are together in emptiness, why do the manifested bodies still remain upon the earth?
Now, the answer is given:

At that time, the assembly had already heard how the Gate of Traces opened the provisional teachings and first entered the land of Quiescent Light; therefore, this was represented by dwelling in space.
As for the manifested traces of the divided bodies, each has its own land of transformation; therefore, these were represented by dwelling on the ground.
Furthermore, Śākyamuni will soon manifest his original state, and he likewise first dwells in emptiness to signify it; each has its own underlying purpose, so there is no need for doubt.

Regarding the passage "At that time, Śākyamuni" and below, the opening of the provisional (the *upāya*) is also discussed in terms of what is signified: Many Treasures came specifically to testify to the sutra and ought to be seen by the assembly. The Buddha’s body signifies the real (*tattva*), while the opening of the stupa signifies the provisional; thus, opening the stupa signifies the opening of the provisional, and seeing the Buddha signifies the manifestation of the real.
If someone were to establish the theory of "Original and Traces" (*honjaku*) based on this, it would be incorrect.
The original text follows below: Question:

Generally speaking, the "Original" (*hon*) should be superior to the "Traces" (*saku*). Looking at the lower section of the "Original Gate," Śākyamuni manifests the Original while Vairocana remains a Trace. Why, then, would the Trace be superior and the Original inferior?
Answer: This interpretation is not correct.

Vairocana is the trace within traces; when viewed from the perspective of his own original state, he is the fundamental [Dharmakāya]. Once Śākyamuni has manifested the trace, it is considered wondrous relative to that trace. Although Vairocana’s trace is wondrous, even this "wondrousness of the trace" is still relatively coarse, as is fully detailed in the tenfold wondrousness of the Introductory Chapter of the *Mysterious Meaning* (Xuanyi).
Regarding the passage in the *Sūtra* from "seeing the two" to "sitting cross-legged," the *Dharmapada-śāstra* states:
"This is to manifest that the three bodies accomplish the great task."

Regarding "eighty-two thousand": eighty thousand are at the beginning of the "Dharma Master" chapter (*dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*), and twenty thousand are at the head of the "Upholding" chapter (*parīndanā-parivarta*). As for the "second eight and a half verses on the gathering of the emanated Buddhas" within the gāthās, there were seven [verses] in the preceding prose; the present verse is extremely concise and does not follow the original sequence.

The second [section] consists of the first three lines of verse, which should be gathered [as follows]: its meaning encompasses Mahāpratibhāna’s desire to see [the Buddha] and his request for the assembly;
next, one line of verse concerns the purification of the land;
and next, four and a half lines of verse concern the simultaneous arrival of all Buddhas.

Regarding the difficulty of upholding [the teachings], the *Sūtra* states that "eighty-four thousand [teachings] are all inferior [to this]. The designation "eighty-four thousand" does not necessarily imply they are entirely minor; as fully cited in the first commentary on the *Zhi Guan*, it refers to scriptures such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Bao'en jing*. Furthermore, even the twelve divisions of the canon encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles, as detailed in the section on the "Excellence of the Dharma-teaching" in the *Xuanwen*: "To cause others merely to attain the six minor supernatural powers is not yet considered difficult, let alone establishing them at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This passage uses those who have not attained penetration as a point of comparison; thus, we know that to briefly read or briefly expound the Perfect Sūtra is truly no easy task.

Regarding the statement, "If there is one who can uphold it, they uphold the Buddha-body," this refers to the three aspects of essence, doctrine, and function, as well as the three items of robe, seat, and chamber, which constitute the three bodies (trikāya).

In the commentary on the *Śakraparivarta*, specifically in the fourth section of the commentary, there is no mention of "contemplating the mind" (*guanxin*); since the initial section on causes and conditions speaks only of the general principle of resonance and response (*yinggan*), it says, "at the time of birth," and so forth.
Question:
When an evil person appears in the world, how can this be called a "response" (yinggan)? Answer:
It causes immeasurable people not to dare commit evil.
Regarding the phrase "the heat of heaven," this is merely spoken in terms of its function.
Question:
Question: Why are there not four *siddhāntas*? Answer:
They are not absent in terms of their established meaning. When a practitioner rejoices that they themselves have not committed [the offense], this is the *loka-siddhānta*.
Not producing wholesome births is itself humanity;
not engaging in the extremes of evil is itself the remedial counteraction;
the state of being unobstructed regarding the fruit is itself the ultimate truth.

Regarding "causal practice" (*hetu-caryā*), the teaching is categorized as follows: in principle, it conforms to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); in fact, it is contrary to the other three teachings. Only in the Perfect Teaching is contrariety itself equivalent to conformity; this is because, in the remaining three teachings, the distinction between contrariety and conformity is fixed.

Regarding the statement in the *Benjì* (Profound Meaning) that [the Buddha] is the same as those who suffer from illness, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Devadatta will certainly not cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
The *Baoen jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states:
"If anyone were to say that Devadatta was truly an evil person who entered the Avīci Hell, such a thing is impossible."
The *Mahāmegha-sūtra* states:
"Devadatta is inconceivable; the karmic practices he cultivates are identical to those of the Tathāgata.

All extant editions, both old and new, state that this chapter was not originally translated by Kumārajīva. Furthermore, according to the catalogs of the Qi and Song dynasties, the śramaṇa Śīladhara (Shi Fayi) of Waguan Monastery obtained a Sanskrit manuscript from the Kingdom of Khotan via the monk Dharmadatta (Shi Faxian) of Shangdinglin Monastery. It was translated and completed in the twelfth month of the eighth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty (492 CE), and it subsequently circulated independently.

At the beginning of the Liang dynasty, there was Dharma Master Man, who had lectured on the sutra one hundred times. He performed self-immolation at the monastery and placed this chapter before the "Chapter on Upholding" (*Chih-pin*); however, it did not yet circulate throughout the world.

At the end of the Liang dynasty, there was a śramaṇa from the kingdom of Western India named Kuṇāladatta, which in Chinese is translated as Zhendi (Paramārtha), who retranslated this chapter and placed it after the "Jeweled Stūpa" chapter.

Now, if one follows the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this chapter already existed during the Western Jin period when that translation was made; thus, it is not the case that the Sanskrit original lacked it.
Furthermore, if one examines the translated text, it closely resembles the literary style of Kumārajīva.

If one follows Jiaxiang’s threefold assessment, first: according to foreign traditions, this chapter has largely been absent from the region east of the Flowing Sands; it is therefore feared that Master Kumārajīva may not have seen it.
Now it is said that Master Kumārajīva personally traveled through the Five Indias; how could he have gone merely as far as the Flowing Sands?
Furthermore, in his translations of the scriptures, Master Kumārajīva often favored brevity, such as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*.
This is also not the case. While Western traditions favor brevity and thus omit redundant material, how could they possibly eliminate an entire chapter of the original text?

Furthermore, if the *Bao ta pin* (Treasure Stūpa Chapter) were intended for the *Chi pin* (Chapter on Upholding), as the third [tradition] claims, and the *Ti po pin* (Devadatta Chapter) were inserted in between, this would result in a completely superfluous scripture; why then would it be placed here?

The current text does not state that it is a retranslation by Paramārtha, nor does it mention Southern Peak (Nanyue) or Sīlabbata. If it were indeed a retranslation by Paramārtha without error, why would it be problematic for the original translation not to have existed previously in Jiangdong?

Judging by this evidence, it appears that all three individuals were in agreement with the underlying principles; thus, the three meanings of "auspiciousness" (*jiāxiáng*) cannot be relied upon at all.
Master Shè stated:

"It is improper to place this here; the 'Prediction for Devadatta' should be placed within the 'Chapter on the Prediction for Those in Training and Those Beyond Training,' and after the 'Chapter on Zhìjī' (Jiànzhī), the 'Chapter on Supernatural Powers' should be placed."

Now, if that were the case, then Kumārajīva of Khotan should have brought two handfuls of scriptures; otherwise, there would be the fault of Dharmayaśas having added [text] to it. If this were so, why is it that in the "Record of Learners and Non-learners," those who are non-learners are included among the twelve hundred, while learners are treated as a separate category? Furthermore, since Devadatta did not claim to have attained the fruits [of the path], why was he suddenly placed among the learners and non-learners?
Regarding the phrase "both preserved and both lost," the text states:
"This sutra was translated five years ago.
Master Dong’an said:
Completed on the sixteenth day of the third month of the seventh year.
This is the same as Huiyuan’s preface to the sutra. Some say:
The translation was completed in the second month of the tenth year of Hongshi.
It is impossible to trace the differences [between the versions].

Zhu Fahu finished his translation on the eleventh day of the eighth month in the first year of Taikang; it consists of eleven fascicles and is titled *Zhengfahua*, though it is also said to be eight fascicles. This is recorded in the catalogue of Nie Daozhen, and these two are the extant versions.
Next was the śramaṇa Zhi Daogen, who translated it into five fascicles in the first year of the Xiankang era of the Jin dynasty, titled "Fangdeng Fahua.

The foreign śramaṇa Zhi Qiangliangjie translated it at Jiaozhou in the seventh month of the first year of the Ganlu era of the Wei dynasty; the śramaṇa Shi Daofu acted as the scribe, producing six fascicles titled "Fahua Samādhi," which appears in the Yao lu and the Wei lu.
Wuqiu Daoliang said: "There are five versions;
four are as previously mentioned, and there is additionally the version of the *Sārvabhaumavibhūti-sūtra*, which still exists in the world, thus making three extant versions."

Regarding the phrase "Ei opened up nine tracks": as soon as Kumārajīva finished his translation, Sengrui lectured upon it, opening it into nine tracks; thus, people of the time called him the Dharma Master of the Nine Tracks.
The first is the track of the mutual resonance between the deluded and the sage, which is the "Preface Chapter" (Xùpǐn).
Next are seven tracks that constitute the "Correct Main Body" (Zhèngzōng): the first is the track of entering the teachings to return to the truth, for those of superior faculties;
the second is the track of manifesting through the emergence of categories, for those of middling faculties.
Third, by recounting the tracks of past experiences—both in adversity and success—the intermediate-capacity followers attain understanding;
fourth, by manifesting the tracks for advancing toward awakening for the sake of those of inferior capacity, it is like bestowing the prediction of enlightenment at the "Transformation City";
fifth, by praising the tracks of his journey, it refers to the "Dharma Master" chapter, wherein he acts as the Tathāgata’s messenger.

The sixth is the "Trace and Source of Non-arising," which corresponds to the *Prabhūtaratna* chapter: Prabhūtaratna does not perish and Śākyamuni is not born; Prabhūtaratna is the source and Śākyamuni is the trace. Since the source does not perish, how could the trace have any arising?
Although the original and the manifested differ, they are inconceivably one.

Seventh, by citing the cause to inquire about the result, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" immediately emerges; Maitreya cites the cause to inquire about the result, while the Buddha cites the lifespan as the basis for that cause and result.
The eighth [section], "Praising the Distant Rescue," concludes with the act of rejoicing (*anumodana*), which belongs to the stage of circulation (*pravartana*).
While its titles are most elegant, its fundamental essence (*śarīra*) is not manifest.

Master Rui also composed a "Genesis of the Twenty-eight Chapters," which provides a clear structural framework and poses no obstacle today; however, the purport of the chapters remains unclarified. Furthermore, since it does not explicitly state that the source is from the *Fayuan* (Dharmapada), but merely speaks of cause and effect, how can it be considered a revelation of the origin?
"The 'Four Great Rivers' (sì dú)" refers to the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Huai, and the Ji.
This implies that all under heaven is one.
Regarding the passage from "Devadatta" to "committing the five heinous crimes," the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha.
Regarding the first of these, "causing a schism in the Saṃgha," it is briefly as explained previously in the account of Maudgalyāyana and in the first commentary on the *Zhiguan*.
Regarding "shedding blood," it is as the Buddha told Śāriputra at Lake Anavatapta:
"In a former age, in Rājagṛha, there was an elder named Sudatta, whose wealth consisted of the seven treasures; his son was named Sumati."
After his father’s death, his half-brother named Sūyasa will be there; Sumati, you must devise a plan so that he does not receive a share of the wealth, and you shall only then kill him.
He then said to his younger brother, "Let us go to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain; there is something to be discussed.
His brother immediately agreed.
He then took his younger brother by the hand, led him to the edge of a precipice, pushed him over the cliff, and crushed him with a stone so that he died on the spot.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The elder at that time was this Great King; Sumati was myself; and the half-brother was Devadatta."

Because of these causes and conditions, for countless thousands of kalpas I entered among the hungry ghosts and fell into the Saṃjīva Hell. Due to the remaining karmic conditions, as I was walking up and down on Vulture Peak Mountain, Devadatta took a stone three zhang long and one zhang six chi wide from a high precipice and hurled it at my head.

"The deity of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain was named Vīra; he caught the stone with his hand, but a small fragment splintered off and fell, wounding the Buddha’s thumb and causing blood to flow from the Buddha.
This is from the *Candraprabha-kumāra-avadāna* (The Sutra on the Arising of Deeds).
The instruction to Aśoka to release the intoxicated elephant and so forth is fully detailed in the third fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Jingangjing*).
The remaining passages may be seen therein;
they are listed in full in various sutras and śāstras.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, in the "Chapter on Karma," states: "All five are subsumed under karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).

Regarding location, they exclude those from the northern continent; regarding persons, they exclude the *śaṇḍha* (eunuchs). Four are bodily actions and one is vocal action; three are killings and one is false speech. One is the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for killing. They ripen over one *kalpa* of the Avīci hell. As the offenses increase, so do the sufferings. Entering the ranks of the bhikṣus is divided into two [categories], which constitute the 'schism of the Saṃgha' (*saṃghabheda*)."

Regarding the phrase "if one acts," and so forth, it is as stated in the text: Devadatta committed only three of the immediate transgressions—schism, expulsion, and killing—but when combined with the two preparatory acts of releasing the elephant and using poisoned claws, these preparatory acts are included, and thus it is said there are five.

The treatise states that there are five types of actions similar to the *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses: namely, defiling one’s mother or an *aśaikṣī* nun; killing a Bodhisattva established in the determination [for enlightenment] or a *śaikṣa* noble one; killing a *śaikṣa* noble one; killing a person who is a counterpart to an Arhat; and seizing the conditions for the harmony of the Saṃgha, which is the counterpart to causing a schism in the Saṃgha;
and destroying a *stūpa*, which is the counterpart to shedding [the Buddha’s] blood.
The reason he does not consider the elephant with its poisonous claws to be of the same class is that [the act of subduing it] was a skillful means (*upāya*) and therefore not of the same class.
The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* asks:
"Devadatta has been the Buddha’s enemy life after life; why then is he called a great bodhisattva?"
The *Śāstra* answers:
"If they were enemies, how could they encounter one another life after life?
It is like two people walking toward the east and west respectively; as they go step by step, they become increasingly distant. How could they ever be companions?"
These five *ānantarya* offenses shall be explained according to their causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Regarding the passage "If one commits [them]," the distinction between the original and the manifested (*honji-suijaku*) has already been briefly discussed in the annotations to the preceding title.

As for the subsequent section beginning with "This chapter," which separately clarifies the purpose of its appearance, an examination of Kasyapa’s three points reveals that they are entirely without merit.

Regarding the phrase "can be known by the mind" followed by "and so forth," one should reiterate that Mañjuśrī is a great bodhisattva who wanders freely; throughout the ten directions he propagates the sutras, even entering the ocean, yet he always proclaims only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Furthermore, regarding all Mahāyāna sutras, Mañjuśrī serves as the catalyst for the assembly.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the perfections" (*pāramitārtha*) and so forth: from the fifteenth chapter through the twenty-first of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the six perfections are explained in detail; within each perfection, numerous interpretations are preserved, of which I have now compiled the general outline.
Those textual characteristics that are prominent are divided into four categories, nor are they arranged in sequence in a single location.
If one wishes to know them in detail, one should consult the original text of the treatise.

Various schools have adopted and rejected [elements] to establish extensive systems of doctrine, citing both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sources indiscriminately so as to provide evidence; thus, it remains unknown which among these constitute the complete practice of Śākyamuni. Only by establishing the teaching according to this single school can the essence and characteristics [of his practice] be recognized.
The traces manifest the four marks, while the fundamental practice is solely perfect. Regarding the first three [categories] within the Tripiṭaka, there are two parts:
first, a brief explanation; second, a detailed analysis.
The first part also has two sub-sections:

First, the six characteristics are directly explained; next, the ten wholesome actions are condensed into the six perfections. Since these six perfections belong to the mundane sphere, they are here contrasted with the ten mundane wholesome actions.

Regarding the subsequent analysis, the *Śīla-sūtra* (*Bhadraśīla-sūtra*) is cited to distinguish three types; in the text, the counteractive measures are first clarified, which refers to that which is to be remedied.
Next, the sequential arising is explained according to the order of practice.

Regarding the term "endowed" (*ju*) within the context of karmic fruition, it means that the sense faculties are complete; "form" refers to being upright and handsome, while "strength" pertains to diligence.
As for the phrase "if one says," the six items each having ten names are found in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (Dichichi) and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Huayan).

Regarding those who belong to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) within the *Candragarbha-sūtra*, it first rebukes the worldly mind and subsequently instructs one to rely upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) to accomplish the *pāramitās*. This means that if one simply takes up a single thought-moment of the initial resolve as being fully complete, then every form and every fragrance is none other than the ten *pāramitās*.

In the phrase "Avataṃsaka," the profound stages of that [other] teaching's path are borrowed to certify the initial mind of the person of the Perfect Teaching; thus, one may verify that the *Avataṃsaka* exists within the teaching path, and its distinct meaning is clearly established.
If one speaks in terms of the ultimate perfection, how could the ten [perfections] be fully present only upon reaching the seventh stage?

Therefore, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it is stated that each thought-moment possesses all ten; the differences between the opening and closing of the six and the ten are as detailed in the seventh fascicle of the *Zhi guan fu xing zhuan hong jue*.
If each thought-moment is endowed with the ten [perfections], what practice or thought would not be endowed with them?
This is what is meant by "one practice encompasses all practices.

When the sutras use the upholding of Prajñāpāramitā as a standard for comparison, stating that it surpasses the sacrifice of bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, this is merely speaking of ultimate practice in contrast to the literal, phenomenal sacrifice.

If all six were the dharma-dhātu, this would not be the case; therefore, one cannot compare them to the three things being entirely empty, nor to the successive production of various conditioned phenomena.

Furthermore, the various passages concerning these six perfections, both high and low, are not without brief explanations; yet, observing the intent of the text, each matter is distinct. If one views them horizontally within the introduction, they merely manifest signs to provoke Maitreya’s doubt;
Mañjuśrī’s citations of the past and his various remarks serve only to lead [the discussion] toward a common understanding.

The Chapter on Past Buddhas opens the way for the five vehicles; however, the text concerning the Bodhisattvas’ six perfections is extremely brief. In the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," the three stages of the Bodhisattva are mentioned without describing their specific practices. The intent there is to distinguish between difference and non-difference, and while the merits are analyzed by briefly citing the six perfections as a basis for comparison, this is not the primary purpose; therefore, no specific methods of practice are provided.

Although the scriptural text herein provides only a brief enumeration, it precisely clarifies the characteristics of the causes of practice and the attainment of the fruit; therefore, the commentator has set them forth in detail so that all practices may converge into the One Vehicle.
Regarding the "thirty-two marks," the various teachings list different methods for their cultivation and attainment, most of which pertain to the path of instruction (*śāsana-mārga*);
as for the true path (*bhūta-mārga*), these marks are simply manifested upon arising and do not require separate cultivation.

As in the verses of praise spoken by the Dragon Girl to the Buddha, how could one who has not deeply penetrated this truth be able to possess the complete marks? This has already been briefly explained in the first fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan* (*Great Calming and Contemplation*) regarding the arising of the bodhicitta through the perception of the marks.

Although the current text explicitly addresses the four marks, its intent lies in their manifestation; therefore, the subsequent passage states: "The true mark is the fundamental characteristic of the Perfect Teaching; although cultivation and manifestation may not be equal, the essence of the marks is for the most part the same."

The current text is mostly found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and also in various other sūtras; once the names have been fully listed according to the *Fajie Cidi*, there remain similarities and differences between this text and those sources. Specifically, this text includes two additional marks not present in the *Fajie Cidi*: the straightness of the heels and the non-visibility of the ankles; furthermore, the radiance on the neck, the *svastika* mark, and the blue hair—these five marks are absent from the *Fajie Cidi*. Conversely, the *Fajie Cidi* contains two marks that are not in this text: the fathom-wide radiance and the moisture in the throat.
The eighty minor marks are also not the same; they merely represent different translations of the sūtras and śāstras.

Regarding the phrase "not a transformation-born being among those born from womb, egg, moisture, or transformation," this is not the same as the transformation-born beings within the four modes of birth in the mundane realms. For instance, even though the gods are transformation-born, they are still born upon the knees of their fathers and so forth; how much less could they be identical to those within the four destinies?
Now, this [birth] occurs suddenly, as it is said in the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*:
"He was suddenly born by transformation in the house of King Śuddhadeva.

Regarding the mention of "moisture-born" and "egg-born," it is simply because the lotus flower remains in a moist state, unopened like moisture or an egg; since he is contained within the flower, the meaning is that he is like an embryo (*garbha*).
The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they will be born by transformation upon a lotus flower in the presence of all Buddhas:

first, not speaking of the faults of others even at the cost of one's life; second, transforming others to lead them to take refuge in the Triple Gem; third, establishing all beings in the bodhicitta; fourth, practicing the Brahma-faring without defilement; fifth, fashioning images of the Buddha and placing them upon flower-adorned seats; sixth, being able to remove the grief and affliction of sentient beings; seventh, always remaining humble before those who are arrogant; and eighth, not causing distress to others."
Although this single sūtra is thus, it is merely taught according to the specific requirements of various sūtras and śāstras.

Even if all the accounts of the causes for the birth of the lotus found in the sūtras and śāstras were to be listed, they would all be surpassed by the merit of the "Chapter on Hearing" in this present text; therefore, while the blooming of the flower is the same, the underlying conditions for each case are distinct.
The phrase "and so forth" may also serve to resolve an objection, but it is not the intended meaning of the present text.
From "At that time, Mañjuśrī... onwards is the third section, "Seeking [the Buddha]. Someone asks:
In the introduction, you were seated here; how is it that you are now said to have come from the ocean?
I shall answer this for you now.
How could one fathom the realm of the sages with ordinary sentiments?
If they do not arise from this assembly to transform sentient beings in the ocean [of existence], what fault would there be in that principle?

Furthermore, having completed their benefit for one period in the introductory section, why would they need to announce their departure when leaving? When they arrive, great benefit arises, and they come from the ocean with the multitude. If we follow the analogy of the Bodhisattvas who sprang forth from the earth and the eulogies therein, the wording of this sutra is extremely concise; perhaps in that version there was an extensive text containing the words regarding their departure from the assembly, while what has been transmitted here is merely an abridgment.
Question:
Beyond the three thousandfold world system, there are each four million billion [worlds] where there are no longer great oceans; why does Mañjuśrī nevertheless say that the ocean has come? Answer:
If even the explanation of these physical matters does not conflict with reason, how much less so for that which is inconceivable?

Now, three points clarify this: first, since both devas and humans have been moved and the great ocean has been transformed, the distance from the place they were moved to where they now appear should not be excessively far.

Second, even if the oceanic assembly were to shift, the Dragon Palace would remain unmoved; yet while the dragons perceive it as unmoved, their dwelling has already been transformed. What is so inconceivable about coming from a place that is transformed yet remains unchanging?

Third, those without karmic connection were transported away, while those with karmic connection have now arrived. This inconceivable mountain and sea were made such that the multitude could not see them; this was merely a transformation of appearance rather than a change in substance. Since Mañjuśrī did not depart from his original place, that land likewise shifted from being defiled to being pure. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "He moved [the assembly] to another land, yet caused no one to have the perception of coming or going. In this instance, however, there is the perception of coming and going, even though there was originally no movement.

Therefore, we know that for those who possess the karmic conditions (*pratyaya*), the earth transforms and the multitudes shift, yet they still arrive; whereas for those who lack such conditions, the earth returns to its original state and the multitudes come but do not arrive.

Thus, although in principle there is no movement, the manifestation of transformations follows a fixed pattern; this causes what is perceived to differ and the timing of arrivals to vary. If even the transformative ritual of a Bodhisattva is thus, how could the transformations established by a Buddha be the same as those of ordinary beings?
Question:
Since he went without arising, why is it said that he "came"? Answer:

This is shown to demonstrate that the assembly understands the power of the sūtra and recognizes the benefit of receiving its teachings; thus, it is necessary to say "he comes. Since he goes where he does not go and comes from where he does not come, all of this is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings—why then should such an objection be raised?

Therefore, we know that other lands do not necessarily appear here; they do not come here, nor does this world go there. Yet, the shifting of events occurs with absolute certainty despite this coming and going.
It is like when Vimalakīrti pressed the earth with his toe: at that moment, the great assembly saw themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers, while the land remained as filthy as before.
In the sūtra, the dragon girl praised by Mañjuśrī does not explicitly mention her vows, meditative concentration, wisdom, or various practices.

"Wisdom" and what follows constitute wisdom (*prajñā*); "deeply entering" and so forth constitute meditative concentration (*samādhi*); "compassionate mindfulness" and so forth constitute her vows; and "merit" and what follows constitute her practice (*caryā*).
There are similar instances throughout the subsequent texts; one should understand them according to this principle.
Regarding the statement within the section correctly demonstrating the perfect fruit that "the dragon girl became a Buddha," a question is raised:
Does she attain Buddhahood without abandoning the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence)?
If one does not attain Buddhahood in this very body, how can the passage concerning the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood and the verses of the *Garbha-sūtra* be reconciled?

Answer: The current text regarding the Dragon Girl speaks from the perspective of expedient means (*upāya*) in order to demonstrate the swiftness of attaining Buddhahood according to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). If one were to practice according to reality, it would not be swift; if one follows mere expedients, they lead nowhere. Thus, the principles of expedient and real meanings are equal, and their logic is not in vain. Therefore, the verses of the *Garbha-sūtra* speak from the perspective of attaining [Buddhahood] through reality.

If one truly attains it, through the purification of the six sense faculties, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); according to the inclinations of sentient beings, one may manifest spiritual transformations, appearing as a Buddha and realizing the Perfect Sūtra.
Having already realized non-arising, how could one not know that fundamentally there is neither abandonment nor sensation? What hindrance is there to abandoning this and proceeding to that?
It is likewise so when those in the stage of ordinary beings in other teachings enter this assembly and advance to sever ignorance.
In all such cases, one must maintain the non-duality of the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*) in order to resolve doubts and obstacles.

Regarding the term "provisional skillfulness" (*upāya-kuśala*), it does not necessarily mean that one should provide exclusively a provisional interpretation. To simply state that the dragon girl has already attained the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is to discuss skillfulness in terms of essence and function (*tattva-vṛtti*); it does not mean that skillfulness is discussed solely in terms of origin and manifestation (*honji-suijaku*). Therefore, both the meanings of the provisional and the real are established through the power of the sūtra.
Other commentators explain this by referring to the seventh or tenth bhūmi and so forth; however, such interpretations fail to manifest the power and function of the sutra.

Regarding the "Chapter on Upholding" (*Dhāraṇī-parivarta*), there are editions that read it as "Exhortation to Uphold. Both meanings must be preserved, as either suits the title. Yet, following the original [title] is preferable; thus, the text is divided into two sections. If one wishes to establish the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) for this passage: explaining both [meanings] together corresponds to the *laukika* (worldly); the twenty thousand [lines] correspond to the *pauruṣeya* (human/edifying); the eighty thousand [lines] correspond to the *prātipākṣika* (remedial); and the Buddha’s intention corresponds to the *paramārtha* (ultimate).

Therefore, the Buddha’s intention was to point to both sections simultaneously; however, within the context of the nuns’ request for a prediction, this passage should be divided into four parts: first, each of the two nuns has their respective request and prediction; second, all the nuns receive understanding and realization; third, all the nuns express their comprehension; and fourth, all the nuns make a vow.
Regarding the term "maternal aunt" mentioned in the *Sūtra*, the *Saṃyukta-nikāya-vastu* (The Collection of Past Deeds) states:
"The Śākya clan member Suprabuddha fathered eight daughters; at that time, King Śuddhodana’s four brothers each took two of these daughters as wives."
"The Queen Mother of King Śuddhodana was Māyā and Āmṛtā.
Māyā passed away seven days after giving birth and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; Āmṛtā was his maternal aunt, and is therefore called 'Aunt-Mother'."
Next is the question and answer.

In the response, it says: "To lead those who have just begun their practice and to open the way for the Practice of Peaceful Abiding. This means that even when practitioners at the initial stage see various great virtuous ones, they are still unable to propagate this sutra in this land; how much more so is this the case for people like us?
Therefore, one must take the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (*Anle-xing-pin*) as the guide for initial practice.
How could one, before the lower part has even emerged, prematurely speak of the practices of the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" (*Yongchu-pin*)?

If that were so, at the beginning of this chapter, Mañjuśrī should have asked the Bodhisattva Saṃcodana what practice he should perform; why did he instead say only "in the future evil age" and so forth?
Furthermore, upon suddenly hearing the name "Saṃcodana," the assembly should have asked who this Saṃcodana was.
As for the subsequent verses, they are independent stanzas (*gāthā*).

In these, the bodhisattvas and others request protection for the propagation of the sutra; this is precisely their own account of the methods for propagating the sutra, as the Buddha had already finished explaining those methods in the "Dharma-Preacher" chapter (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*).

The *Ratnakoṭi* (Jewel Tower) seeks those who employ the correct method (*mārga*), while the *Sadāprarudita* (Ever-Weeping) guides those who are led by the correct method; Śākyamuni is himself one among the assembly that has received this correct method, which is why it says, "He uses his own body as a bed and seat," and so forth.

The "Chapter on Upholding" (*Dhāraṇī-paṭala*) constitutes the method for the degenerate age, while the "Peaceful Practices" (*Sukhavihāra*) constitutes the method for those beginning their practice; thus it says, "Abiding on the ground of patience," and so forth, as detailed in the subsequent chapters.

If it were not so, then the propagation of the sutras would lack a proper method; for there is no such possibility as propagating the sutras without a method—just as it is not in vain for one to suffer injury by entering a battle naked, the words regarding the donning of armor must surely not have been spoken in vain.
The first seventeen lines consist of three sections regarding the wearing of the robe of patience (*kṣānti-vastra*):

first, one line provides a general discussion of the timing to clarify the act of donning the robe; next, nine lines beginning with "There are those... specifically clarify the objects of patience; and finally, seven lines beginning with "We... clarify the intention for wearing the robe.
The first part is as in the text. The second part consists of three sections:
first, one line generally clarifies those of heterodox views, namely the worldly multitude;
next, one line clarifies those with overweening pride within the Way.
Regarding those who practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment while being arrogant and overestimating themselves as sages:
among these three types, the first may be tolerated; the second is worse than the former; and the third is most severe, because each subsequent type becomes increasingly difficult to recognize.
The first two [sections] are as written in the text.
Regarding the third section, the reference to "the sixth *āraṇyaka* of the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*" and so forth is likely an error; the text is actually found in the fifth [section].
First, to explain the names: "A" means "non-existence.
"Aranya" is translated as "contention" (*raṇa*); in the text it is referred to as "affairs," for because there are affairs, there is contention.
Now, following the sūtra, we shall first set forth correct practice and subsequently distinguish what is erroneous.

The initial passage states: "One who dwells in an araṇya does not contend with the world; it should be neither too near nor too far for the sake of alms-gathering; it should have tree shade, abundant flowers and fruits, and sufficient pure water; it should be free from difficulties, not rugged or treacherous, and easy to access; one should dwell alone without companions, reciting what has been heard, and so forth."
If kings, ministers, elders, or others come seeking him out, he should say:
"Welcome, welcome!

When you arrive at my dwelling, I should invite you to sit; I must not sit alone. If you do not accept a humble seat, I should comfort you in various ways and preach the Dharma for you. If you do not wish for an extensive explanation, I should provide a brief one," and so forth.
If it were not so, it would not be the practice of an araṇya-dweller.

One who dwells in an araṇya does so to subdue the afflictions; to exalt oneself and despise others is not the practice of non-contention. I do not yet understand where your intention lies in merely sitting with hands folded.

He treats his teachers and friends with contempt and is arrogant toward kings and ministers; how much more so does he cause the ignorant to claim him a sage, making those with eyes shudder with cold? Rāhula’s conduct has forever strayed from the path, and where now is the virtue of Śūnyatājanman?

It is simply because the mind lacks internal substance and devotes itself exclusively to external pursuits through the body; when one earnestly examines the Way, there is nothing at all to be said. This is clearly illustrated by Pindola knowing his kingdom would be lost after seven years, and by Master Tanyou’s advancement or refusal to become king; therefore, in managing one's daily life, one must adapt to the times—how could one possibly remain fixed in a single direction?

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* clarifies that an araṇya bhikṣu must possess fifty qualities before he is fit to dwell [in the forest], and even for each of the twelve dhūtas, there are ten specific qualities; otherwise, one should instead seek out a teacher to advance on the Path—why hastily cling to ignorance?

Regarding the phrase "should not follow the formal rules": those who have left the household life to renounce the world, sever their attachments, and seek the Way ought to take the fivefold precepts as their standard of correctness. If they already violate the formal rules of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and instead treat the Great Teaching (Mahāyāna) with contempt, the harm is all the more severe.

If one applies this name uniformly to the Great [Vehicle], then the three trainings and two liberations of the Perfect Vehicle can serve as a self-regulation, which should correspond to the monastic model of the forest hermitage (araṇya).

Regarding the passage from "Although they speak" to "attaining livelihood," this refers to those who cling to what they have been taught but do not diligently practice it, focusing instead solely on their own survival; such individuals as these are said to possess a semblance of the three trainings (*triśikṣā*). They are a counterfeit of the three trainings, a thief of the three trainings, and a fraud regarding the three trainings. Because they seek to disparage those who have mastered the sūtras, this causes the propagators [of the Dharma] to don the armor of patience and single-mindedly propagate the True Dharma.

Only when a person who possesses the precepts increases all three trainings can they be called one who "increases the precepts. If one merely guards the one [precept] without practicing it, one knows that the precepts are diminished; if one does not even practice the precepts, how could one peacefully practice concentration and wisdom?
Therefore, one must examine this by traversing five sections.

Regarding the intent of the three types of robes, the passage cited from the *Madhyama Āgama*, chapter five, concerning the monk Kāḷodāyin’s petition to the Buddha, corresponds to the text on the "five departures" of persons found in the third chapter of that same *Madhyama Āgama*.
In that sutra, the *Jalopama-sūtra* from the *Śāriputra-saṃyukta-varga*, it is said:
"When the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s [Monastery], Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
'I say that there are five conditions for the affliction of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*')."
"What are the five? He then used five metaphors to illustrate the three types of action (trikarma).

Upon further examining the fifth scripture, the "five persons" are simply the three types of action: those who are exclusively virtuous constitute three; those who are virtuous in both [body and speech] constitute one; and those who are evil in both constitute one. If one further adds those who are virtuous in two [aspects], this forms three additional categories, resulting in eight categories in total.

Regarding the statement that "in the extreme of evil, there can be neither single nor double [factors]": a single instance of good is itself a double instance of evil, and a double instance of good is itself a single instance of evil; therefore, a category belonging exclusively to the extreme of evil cannot exist.
The reason the other three phrases are not mentioned in the sutra is either because it cites five instances to represent eight, or because it adapts to the capacities of the audience.
As for the passage where it initially states that the body is evil while speech and mind are good, this is likely an error.

In the corresponding combined analogies, there is only a single wholesome [action]; therefore, one should simply say: "wholesome body with unwholesome speech and mind," "wholesome speech with unwholesome body and mind," or "wholesome mind with unwholesome body and speech."

Therefore, regarding the initial metaphor of "the patched robe" and so forth, this refers to bodily virtue and the non-virtue of speech and mind; it corresponds to the text which states: "One should contemplate using the body for purification and abandon [non-virtue] in speech and mind."

Regarding "good in speech but not so in the midst": when one parts the grass to avoid the heat, the physical action is not good; yet when one scoops up water, it does not meet with praise, which indicates the intention is not good. Although the water reaches the mouth, it is merely called "good" [in name]. As for the text stating "whether with a scoop or with the hand," this refers simply to scooping with the hand.
The *Qieyun* explains "jù" (掬) as "to take with the hand.
It is also written singly as "jú" (匊).
Although both body and speech are unwholesome, it is called "virtuous in intention" because it serves only to quench thirst.
If one wishes to use an analogy for the three pairs of wholesome qualities, one should reflect upon them by analogy with the single [set].
